title: Ship Attacks Near the Strait of Hormuz Reach a Weekly High
summary:
The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow waterway in the Middle East. Many tankers carry oil through it to the rest of the world. Since the war between the US and Israel and Iran began, ships there have faced attacks.

Twelve ships were reported attacked between October 5 and October 11. That is the highest weekly number reported to the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency since the war started. The week before, 10 ships reported attacks. Six ships were struck on one day, last Sunday. Four more attacks were reported early this week. These numbers are approximate, because some reports use the day of the attack and others the day it was reported.

Experts say Iran has been attacking ships to try to gain more control over the waterway. Meanwhile, the US military has been helping more tankers travel safely through the southern part of the strait. US Navy data shows the number of ships it helped in the first 10 days of October was 85% higher than in the same period in August.

The US military's Central Command said commercial ships are still moving through the strait with protection from US forces and partners. When one container ship sank this week, all 21 crew members were safely evacuated.

The attacks have slowed oil shipments. About 12.6 million barrels a day passed through the strait on October 13, according to the data firm Kpler. That is down from 15 million at the end of September. Before the war, the number was about 17 million.

Iran says ships using a route near Oman's coast are "unauthorised." One security expert said the aim of the attacks is to stop ships and to discourage others from coming.
why_it_matters: Much of the world's oil travels through this waterway, so attacks there can affect fuel supplies and prices far away.

background_read: The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf to the open ocean, and Iran lies along its northern shore.
Many countries in the Gulf region export oil, and much of it must travel by tanker through this narrow passage.
When ships cannot pass safely, less oil reaches world markets, which can push fuel prices up in other countries.
Navies sometimes escort commercial ships through dangerous waters to help protect them from attack.
